title: Two Types of AI News Content
author: Fitzy History
source: Teaching in the Age of AI (fitzyhistory.substack.com), September 7, 2026
summary: A history teacher and education consultant proposes a framework for defusing unproductive AI arguments by sorting all AI commentary into 'inner' content (about the technology itself, consumed by power users who test every new model) and 'outer' content (about AI's effects on people and society, dominated by op-eds on alignment, regulation, and safety). His central diagnostic is that each camp carries a predictable blind spot: outer-content commentators like AI-skeptic Ed Zitron often barely use the technology they're critiquing, while inner-content power users' heavy personal usage creates cognitive dissonance that makes negative findings hard to absorb. Writing from four years straddling both worlds as a teacher who has built two AI-assisted course websites this year, he reports that reading both camps hasn't pushed him toward a comfortable middle position but instead pulled his views apart -- genuinely impressed by what AI now lets him build for his own courses, while growing more alarmed that students are using AI constantly with almost no structured guidance from their institutions. He closes with a practical framework for productive AI conversations: identify which kind of content each party consumes, separate claims about models from claims about companies, and separate claims about AI's current state from claims about its trajectory, while noting the strongest available evidence (a 27,000-student, 30-month Chinese study) currently points toward real learning losses.
points: The inner/outer content framework gives a concrete diagnostic for why AI conversations talk past each other: inner-content consumers evaluate models and capabilities, outer-content consumers evaluate societal and ethical stakes, and each group is largely unaware the other lane exists.

The Ed Zitron example crystallizes the outer-content blind spot: a prominent AI skeptic undermines his own credibility by claiming he 'doesn't really' use AI while admitting in the same interview that he has 'put it through its paces,' making his critique easier to dismiss regardless of its substance.

Two specific claim-separations are offered as tools for de-escalating debates: a claim about a model's capability is not a claim about its maker's conduct, and a claim about AI's current state is not a prediction about where it's heading -- conflating these is identified as the recurring source of talking past one another.

The author's own experience refutes the expectation that balanced exposure produces moderation: reading both camps for four years has pulled his views apart rather than toward a synthesis, being simultaneously more convinced of AI's classroom-productivity value and more alarmed about the near-total absence of structured student guidance.
quotes: On the tech side it was launched as "the world's most intelligent and aligned model," while at the same time critics accused the company of trading away safety monitoring for a modest gain in performance. Which half of that coverage you gravitated toward says more about you than it does about the model.

Inner AI content is created mostly by and for power users who catalogue and test every new model within days of its release. The intense focus on using the technology means inner AI content consumers mostly look inward.

Asked what he uses AI for, he says he really doesn't, though a few sentences later says he has put it through its paces. That is the blind spot, and it costs him credibility with the kind of people who might otherwise be more willing to hear him out.
I assumed reading both would land me somewhere in the middle. It hasn't. My views are pulling apart.
Astra is impressive" and "OpenAI concealed an incident for weeks" are both true. A claim about today is not a claim about the trajectory.

The most substantial recent study we have - a working paper tracking nearly 27,000 Chinese secondary students over 30 months - found real learning losses. The good evidence we do have is mostly negative, but better evidence in either direction is going to take years.
